Developers seek early engineering analysis amid rising costs and regulations, SESI says
A. M. Egan
Developers are increasingly seeking input from engineers before purchasing land or pursuing project approvals as construction costs rise and environmental regulations tighten, according to an Aug. 5 report by Parsippany-based SESI Consulting Engineers. The firm said this shift has made geotechnical, environmental, and civil engineering input central to early development decisions rather than just the design phase.
Company officials said consulting engineers now evaluate site conditions, environmental issues, utility capacity, and construction challenges at the outset of projects to identify potential obstacles and help control costs. “SESI works closely with our clients to develop practical site and entitlement strategies that support their goals while addressing these challenges,” said Franz Laki, principal at SESI Consulting Engineers. “We recognize that no two sites or projects are alike, and each deserves a deliberate, thoughtful, and solutions-oriented approach.”
Founded in 1976, SESI provides geotechnical, environmental and civil engineering services for commercial and infrastructure projects throughout New Jersey, New York, Connecticut and the Northeast. The company said it is increasingly evaluating project feasibility by examining engineering, environmental and construction issues simultaneously rather than in separate phases.
This approach is especially important for redevelopment sites where aging infrastructure or required environmental remediation present additional challenges. As an example of its work on such sites, SESI cited an industrial redevelopment project in Lyndhurst where engineers used ground improvement techniques including surcharge loading and dynamic compaction instead of deep foundations—reducing construction costs while improving buildability. In Fair Lawn, SESI coordinated remediation efforts for redeveloping a former industrial property into a warehouse.
The northeastern United States presents some of the country's most challenging subsurface conditions—such as those found in the New Jersey Meadowlands—with up to approximately 200 feet of compressible marsh deposits along with silts, clays and variable fill materials. SESI has long supported projects requiring specialized ground improvement strategies that reduce foundation risks for developers.
Industry clients say they now expect engineering firms to act as advisers during initial planning stages. "We needed a consultant that would function more like a business partner," said Peter Palazzo, president of LRC Construction LLC in White Plains. "They stayed engaged and adapted as our needs evolved." Looking ahead, SESI expects continued demand for early-stage engineering services across sectors including industrial redevelopment projects.
The New Jersey Business and Industry Association serves as the nation's largest statewide employer association representing private-sector employers throughout New Jersey; it facilitates partnerships among businesses, government entities, and academic institutions; advances members' competitive excellence; offers advocacy information and cost-saving benefits; Michele Siekerka serves as president, according to the official website.
